issues.legal_issue: A final decision by a court of limited pecuniary jurisdiction can bar relitigation of the same issue in a later suit even if the earlier court could not have tried the later suit.
material_facts: An earlier court of limited pecuniary jurisdiction decided an issue that was directly and substantially in dispute.
The same issue was raised in a later suit between the same parties or their privies.
issues.conclusion: Explanation VIII to Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure includes courts of limited pecuniary jurisdiction, so their final decisions can operate as res judicata in later suits even when those courts could not have tried the later suits.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 CPC, read with Explanation VIII, makes a final decision on an issue by a competent court of limited jurisdiction conclusive in a later suit between the same parties or their privies. The Court relied on P.M. Kavade v. A.B. Bokil, Rai Bahadur Singh v. Rai Beni Madho Rakesh Singh, Daryao v. State of U.P., and Gulam Abbas v. State of U.P. in explaining the scope and public-policy basis of res judicata.

rule.if: limited_jurisdiction_prior_decision and issue_finally_decided and later_suit_between_parties_or_privies and same_issue_raised

predicates.limited_jurisdiction_prior_decision: A court whose jurisdiction was limited, including by pecuniary limits, decided the issue in the earlier proceeding.
predicates.issue_finally_decided: The issue was directly and substantially raised and was finally decided in the earlier proceeding.
predicates.later_suit_between_parties_or_privies: A later suit was brought between the same parties or persons claiming through them.
predicates.same_issue_raised: The same issue was directly and substantially raised in the later suit.

issues.definition: When a limited-jurisdiction court has finally decided an issue that is raised again in a later suit between the same parties or their privies, the earlier decision bars relitigation.

issues.legal_issue: A final decision in an injunction suit can bar a later title suit when title was directly and substantially in issue and decided in the injunction suit.
material_facts: In an earlier injunction suit, the court considered the parties’ competing rights in the property and determined the nature of the interest created by a settlement deed.
The injunction decree became final, and the same title issue was raised in a later suit between the parties or their privies.
issues.conclusion: The injunction decree operated as res judicata in the later suit based on title because the title issue had been directly and substantially in issue and decided in the earlier suit.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 CPC applies when title is directly and substantially in issue in an injunction suit and is decided; the equitable nature of the injunction remedy does not prevent the decision from operating as res judicata in a later title suit between the same parties or their privies.

rule.if: injunction_suit and title_directly_in_issue and title_finally_decided and later_title_suit_between_parties_or_privies

predicates.injunction_suit: The earlier proceeding sought an injunction concerning rights in property.
predicates.title_directly_in_issue: The parties’ title or interest in the property was directly and substantially in issue in that proceeding.
predicates.title_finally_decided: The court decided the title or interest issue, and its decision became final.
predicates.later_title_suit_between_parties_or_priv: A later suit based on title was brought between the same parties or persons claiming through them.

issues.definition: A final title decision in an injunction suit bars the same title issue from being relitigated in a later title suit between the same parties or their privies.

issues.legal_issue: A transferee who acquires property from a party while a suit concerning that property is pending is bound by the resulting decision in the circumstances addressed by the court.
material_facts: A purchaser acquired the property from a person who was a party to an earlier suit while that suit was pending.
The purchaser claimed through that party, and the prior decrees addressed rights in the property; a later injunction suit also included the purchaser.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser was bound by the prior decrees as a successor in title and was also affected by the doctrine of lis pendens.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 CPC binds parties and their privies to final decisions on issues directly and substantially determined in earlier proceedings. Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act applies the doctrine of lis pendens to a transfer of property during the pendency of a suit concerning rights in that property.

rule.if: property_suit_pending and transfer_from_party_during_suit and transferee_claims_through_party and prior_decision_finally_determines_property_issue

predicates.property_suit_pending: A suit concerning rights in the property was pending when the transfer occurred.
predicates.transfer_from_party_during_suit: A party to that suit transferred the property while the suit was pending.
predicates.transferee_claims_through_party: The transferee derives the claimed interest from the party who made the transfer.
predicates.prior_decision_finally_determines_proper: The resulting final decision determined an issue concerning rights in the property.

issues.definition: A transferee who acquires property from a party during a pending property suit and claims through that party is bound by a final decision determining rights in the property.

issues.legal_issue: An arbitrator should not be removed for lack of reasonable dispatch when the applicant’s own delay was substantial and the arbitrator’s delay, considered in context, did not justify removal.
material_facts: The party seeking removal of the named arbitrator had previously delayed taking steps in the arbitration and again took no step for a substantial period after receiving notice of a proposed meeting.
The meeting date in the arbitrator’s notice was mistaken, but the party did not ask the arbitrator to fix another meeting.
The arbitrator’s delay, considered against the applicant’s conduct, was not sufficient to establish a lack of reasonable dispatch.
The agreement named a technically qualified arbitrator for a technical construction dispute.
issues.conclusion: The order removing the named arbitrator and appointing another arbitrator was set aside, and the named arbitrator was directed to proceed with the arbitration.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed whether the arbitrator had failed to use reasonable dispatch in the circumstances, taking account of the applicant’s own delays and inaction. It did not decide the separate question whether the parties intended a vacancy to be supplied under Section 8 of the Arbitration Act, and it relied on no earlier case in reaching its factual conclusion.

predicates.appeal_from_arbitrator_removal_order: The proceeding is an appeal from an order removing a named arbitrator and appointing a replacement.
predicates.applicant_delayed_arbitration_steps: The party seeking removal substantially delayed or failed to take available steps to advance the arbitration.
predicates.arbitrator_delay_not_unreasonable_in_con: The arbitrator’s delay, assessed in light of the parties’ conduct and the circumstances, did not amount to unjustifiable lack of dispatch.
predicates.agreement_names_technically_qualified_ar: The agreement names an arbitrator with relevant technical expertise for a technically specialized dispute.

issues.definition: When an applicant seeking removal has delayed advancing the arbitration, the arbitrator’s delay is not unreasonable in context, and the agreement names a technically qualified arbitrator, the removal order is set aside and the named arbitrator continues.
